purposes.src/font/ByteReader.h: Reading big-endian numbers from any position in a font file: unsigned and signed integers of 8, 16 and 32 bits, and F2Dot14 fixed point. Every later assignment that reads the font reads it through this: assignment 02 the table directory, 03 to 05 the `cmap`, `loca` and metrics tables, and 07 and 09 the glyph outlines.
purposes.src/font/ByteReader.cpp: The reader's implementation: opening the file, moving around in it, and turning its bytes into numbers. Every later assignment that reads the font runs through this code, so a mistake here shows up everywhere.
purposes.src/font/FontParser.h: Opening a font and reading its table directory: the tag, checksum, offset and length of every table (`cmap`, `glyf`, `loca`, ...). Assignments 03 to 05 find their tables by tag in these records, and assignment 18 opens the font through it.
purposes.src/font/FontParser.cpp: The code that reads the table directory from the first bytes of the file, through your `ByteReader`. Every later step that needs a table starts from what it reads.
purposes.src/font/Cmap.h: The `cmap` table: which glyph draws each character, read from the format 12 subtable for the full Unicode range. Later, assignment 18 looks up every character of a line of text here.
purposes.src/font/Cmap.cpp: The code that reads the platform 0 / encoding 4 subtable of `cmap` into a character-to-glyph map. Assignment 18 builds this map once per font.
purposes.src/font/Loca.h: The `loca` table: where each glyph's record is in the file and how many bytes it takes, by glyph id. Assignment 09 uses it to find the parts of a compound glyph, and assignment 18 to find the glyph of every character.
purposes.src/font/Loca.cpp: The code that reads `maxp`, `head` and `loca` and works out one location per glyph id. Assignments 09 and 18 look glyphs up in what it returns.
purposes.src/font/Metrics.h: The `hhea` and `hmtx` tables: the font's ascent and descent, and each glyph's advance width and left side bearing. Later, assignment 18 moves the pen by each glyph's advance width and sizes the text from the ascent and descent.
purposes.src/font/Metrics.cpp: The code that reads `hhea`, `maxp` and `hmtx` into the ascent, the descent and one set of metrics per glyph id, including the glyphs that store only a side bearing. Assignment 18 loads it once per font.
purposes.src/FrameBufferCanvas.h: A picture in memory, one colour per pixel, with three ways to draw on it (one pixel, a filled rectangle, a thick line) and a way to save it as a PNG. Every picture from assignment 08 on is drawn on it: outlines in 08 and 11, filled glyphs in 14, 16 and 17, and a line of text in 18.
purposes.src/FrameBufferCanvas.cpp: A picture in memory, one colour per pixel, with three ways to draw on it (one pixel, a filled rectangle, a thick line) and a way to save it as a PNG. Every picture from assignment 08 on is drawn on it: outlines in 08 and 11, filled glyphs in 14, 16 and 17, and a line of text in 18.
purposes.src/GlyphComponent.h: The form every outline takes in the project: its points (x and y in font units, on or off the curve) and the index where each contour ends. Assignments 08 and 11 draw outlines in this form, 09 produces one per part of a compound glyph, and 14, 16 and 17 fill them.
purposes.src/Glyph.h: A glyph as the glyf table stores it: whether it is empty, simple or compound, its contour count, its bounding box and, for a simple glyph, its outline. Your `GlyphParser` returns it, and assignment 09 uses its kind to tell simple glyphs from compound ones.
purposes.src/font/GlyphParser.h: Decoding one glyph record from the glyf table into the types in `Glyph.h`: the header of every glyph, and the contours and points of a simple one. Assignment 09 calls it for every simple glyph a compound glyph is made of.
purposes.src/font/GlyphParser.cpp: Decoding one glyph record from the glyf table into the types in `Glyph.h`: the header of every glyph, and the contours and points of a simple one. Assignment 09 calls it for every simple glyph a compound glyph is made of.
purposes.src/render/Placement.h: Where a glyph goes on the canvas: the pixel column of font x = 0, the pixel row of the baseline and the pixels per font unit, which together turn font units (y up) into pixels (y down). Assignments 11, 14, 16 and 17 place their glyphs with it, and assignment 18 moves it along a line of text, one glyph at a time.
purposes.src/render/Outline.h: Drawing a glyph's outline on the canvas: straight lines between its points and a marker on every point. Assignment 11 adds a second drawing with the real curves to the same files.
purposes.src/render/Outline.cpp: Drawing a glyph's outline on the canvas: straight lines between its points and a marker on every point. Assignment 11 adds a second drawing with the real curves to the same files.
purposes.src/font/CompoundGlyph.h: Turning any glyph into the simple outlines it is drawn with: a compound glyph's components are read, moved, scaled or rotated, and resolved however deeply they nest. Assignment 18 draws every character of a line of text through it, so it never has to tell simple glyphs from compound ones.
purposes.src/font/CompoundGlyph.cpp: Turning any glyph into the simple outlines it is drawn with: a compound glyph's components are read, moved, scaled or rotated, and resolved however deeply they nest. Assignment 18 draws every character of a line of text through it, so it never has to tell simple glyphs from compound ones.
purposes.src/utils/Geometry.h: The project's 2D maths in one header: a point type, lerp, and the point at t on a quadratic Bezier curve. Assignment 11 draws curves with it, assignments 12, 13 and 15 add where segments and curves meet and a curve's lowest point, and the fills from assignment 14 on build on it.
purposes.src/render/Scanline.h: The part of filling that doesn't depend on the rule: an outline turned into edges in pixels and, row by row, where the line through the pixel centres crosses them. Your even-odd fill here and the non-zero fill of assignments 16 and 17 both run on it.
purposes.src/render/Scanline.cpp: The part of filling that doesn't depend on the rule: an outline turned into edges in pixels and, row by row, where the line through the pixel centres crosses them. Your even-odd fill here and the non-zero fill of assignments 16 and 17 both run on it.
purposes.src/render/EvenOdd.h: Filling a glyph by the even-odd rule, on top of `render/Scanline`. Assignment 16 adds the non-zero rule beside it, and that is the one the text renderer of assignment 18 uses.
purposes.src/render/EvenOdd.cpp: Filling a glyph by the even-odd rule, on top of `render/Scanline`. Assignment 16 adds the non-zero rule beside it, and that is the one the text renderer of assignment 18 uses.
purposes.src/render/NonZero.h: Filling a glyph by the non-zero rule, the rule fonts are designed for, on top of `render/Scanline`. This assignment handles straight edges, assignment 17 adds curves, and the text renderer of assignment 18 fills every glyph with it.
purposes.src/render/NonZero.cpp: Filling a glyph by the non-zero rule, the rule fonts are designed for, on top of `render/Scanline`. This assignment handles straight edges, assignment 17 adds curves, and the text renderer of assignment 18 fills every glyph with it.
purposes.src/utils/Unicode.h: Turning UTF-8 text into Unicode code points, the numbers a font's cmap is keyed by. Your `TextRenderer` decodes every line of text with it.
purposes.src/TextRenderer.h: The whole pipeline in one class: a font's tables loaded once, then each character of a line of text mapped to its glyph, filled by the non-zero rule and followed by its advance. The checker's program and `main.cpp` both draw through it.
purposes.src/TextRenderer.cpp: The whole pipeline in one class: a font's tables loaded once, then each character of a line of text mapped to its glyph, filled by the non-zero rule and followed by its advance. The checker's program and `main.cpp` both draw through it.
purposes.src/main.cpp: The finished command-line program: `tiny_ttf <font.ttf> "<text>" <out.png>` draws a line of text with a TrueType font into a PNG sized to fit it, using your `TextRenderer`. An optional fourth argument sets the text height in pixels (64 by default).

book.title: Tiny TrueType Workbook
book.sourceTitle: Writing a tiny TrueType parser and renderer from scratch
book.author: Yohei Yamasaki
book.headline: Build a TrueType renderer yourself
book.lede: Each checkpoint asks you to write the program that one part of the blog post builds, from reading big-endian bytes to drawing a line of text. A checker feeds your program inputs and compares what it writes with answers worked out independently, mostly by fontTools. How you structure the code, and which language or library you use, is up to you.
book.credits: Fonts: JetBrains Mono (Nerd Font build) and Noto Sans JP, both under the SIL Open Font License. Expected outputs come from fontTools. Progress is saved in this browser only.

jobs.assignments/assignment_01_byte_readers.c: Read the `file` line and open that file with your `ByteReader`, then run the other lines in order: `jump` and `skip` move the reader, and each read writes `<op> <value>`. When a read runs out of bytes, write `eof` and stop. The Output section has the format, including how F2Dot14 values may be printed.
jobs.src/font/ByteReader.h: Declare a reader that opens a binary file and keeps a current position. It needs a way to jump to an absolute offset, skip forward, read each of the six integer types (`u8` to `i32`) big-endian, and read an F2Dot14 as a floating-point number, plus a way to report that a read ran out of bytes (an exception type, for example).
jobs.src/font/ByteReader.cpp: Implement the reader: open the file in binary mode, move the position for jumps and skips, and build each number from its bytes, most significant first, with two's complement for the signed types. A read that needs a byte past the end of the file must report it instead of returning a value.

jobs.assignments/assignment_02_table_director: Read the `font` line, read that file's table directory with your `FontParser` code, and write `tables <numTables>` followed by one `table` line per record. The Output section has the exact format, including the quotes around the tag.
jobs.src/font/FontParser.h: Declare a record for one table (its 4-character tag, `checkSum`, `offset` and `length`), a function that reads the whole directory through your `ByteReader`, and a collection of records you can look up by tag, which assignments 03 to 05 use. Assignment 18 also wants one object that opens a font and holds its reader and tables; you can declare it now or then.
jobs.src/font/FontParser.cpp: Implement the directory reader: read `numTables` from the 12-byte header, skipping the other header fields, then read one 16-byte record per table, keeping the tag's 4 bytes exactly as stored. If you declared a font object, have it open the file and load the directory once.

jobs.assignments/assignment_03_cmap.cpp: Read the `font` line, turn the `table "cmap"` line into a table record (you need its offset), and load the character map once with your `Cmap` code. If loading reports no usable subtable, write only `unsupported`; otherwise answer each `count` and `lookup` line in input order, in the formats the Output section gives.
jobs.src/font/Cmap.h: Declare a function that reads a font's character map, given your `ByteReader` and the table records from your `FontParser`, and returns something that can say how many code points are mapped and which glyph id a code point maps to, if any. Also declare how it reports a font without a usable subtable (an exception type, for example).
jobs.src/font/Cmap.cpp: Implement it: find the encoding record with platform 0 and encoding 4, check that its subtable is format 12, and read its groups so that every code point they cover can be looked up. Report the two `unsupported` cases (no such record, or another format) the way your header declares.

jobs.assignments/assignment_04_loca.cpp: Read the `font` line, turn the four `table` lines (`glyf`, `head`, `loca`, `maxp`) into table records, collect the `glyph` ids, and load the locations once with your `Loca` code. Write the `glyphs <numGlyphs> loca <short|long>` line, then one `glyph <id> <offset> <length>` line per requested id, in input order.
jobs.src/font/Loca.h: Declare a glyph location (an offset from the start of the file and a length in bytes) and a function that reads the location of every glyph, given your `ByteReader` and the table records from your `FontParser`. Have its result also carry `numGlyphs` and whether `loca` uses the short or long format, since the first output line needs both.
jobs.src/font/Loca.cpp: Implement it: read `numGlyphs` from `maxp` and `indexToLocFormat` from `head`, read the `numGlyphs` + 1 `loca` entries, and turn them into an absolute offset and a length for each glyph id. The fields and formulas are under "The tables you need".

jobs.assignments/assignment_05_metrics.cpp: Read the `font` line, turn the three `table` lines (`hhea`, `hmtx`, `maxp`) into table records, collect the questions, and load the metrics once with your `Metrics` code. Answer each `font-metrics` and `glyph` line in input order, in the formats the Output section gives.
jobs.src/font/Metrics.h: Declare the metrics of one glyph (advance width and left side bearing) and a function that reads the font's ascent and descent and the metrics of every glyph id, given your `ByteReader` and the table records from your `FontParser`.
jobs.src/font/Metrics.cpp: Implement it: read `ascent`, `descent` and `numberOfHMetrics` from `hhea` and `numGlyphs` from `maxp`, then read `hmtx` so that every glyph id from 0 to `numGlyphs` - 1 gets an advance and an lsb, by the two rules under "A glyph's metrics".

jobs.assignments/assignment_06_canvas.cpp: Read the `canvas` line and create a canvas of that size, then read the `point`, `rect` and `line` commands in order and call the matching canvas operation with each one's colour. At the end, write the picture to the output path (see Output).
jobs.src/FrameBufferCanvas.h: Declare a colour type (red, green and blue, one byte each) and a canvas type that holds a width, a height and one colour per pixel, all black to start. Declare its operations: paint one pixel, draw a filled rectangle from its centre and size, draw a line between two points with a thickness, and write the picture to a file.
jobs.src/FrameBufferCanvas.cpp: Implement those operations as "Painting one pixel", "Drawing a rectangle" and "Drawing a line" describe: painting a pixel ignores anything outside the picture, a rectangle clips its loops to the canvas, and a line stamps a square at every step. Write the pixels out as a PNG with `stbi_write_png`, or as a binary PPM.

jobs.assignments/assignment_07_simple_glyph.c: For each `font` line, open that file with your `ByteReader`. For each `glyph` line, decode the record it points to and write `empty`, `compound`, or the three lines of a simple glyph, as Output shows.
jobs.src/GlyphComponent.h: Declare a point type (x, y and whether it is on the curve) and an outline type that holds the contour end indices and the list of points. Give x and y a type that can hold fractions, such as `double`: assignment 08 reads coordinates like `120.75` and assignment 09 scales points.
jobs.src/Glyph.h: Declare a glyph type that records which of the three kinds it is (empty, simple or compound) and holds `numberOfContours`, the bounding box (`xMin`, `yMin`, `xMax`, `yMax`) and, for a simple glyph, its outline in the form from `GlyphComponent.h`.
jobs.src/font/GlyphParser.h: Declare one function that decodes the glyph record at a given offset and length, reading through your `ByteReader` from assignment 01, and returns a glyph from `Glyph.h`.
jobs.src/font/GlyphParser.cpp: Implement it as "The glyph record you are decoding" lays out: length 0 gives an empty glyph, a negative `numberOfContours` gives a compound glyph with nothing read past the header, and a simple glyph gets its contour ends and every point, with absolute coordinates and its own on/off flag.

08.title: Draw an outline with straight lines

Create the canvas from the `canvas` line and keep the most recent `place`, `style` and `color`. For each `outline`, read its `ends` and `points` (coordinates may be fractional) and draw it; at the end, write the picture to the output path.
jobs.src/render/Placement.h: Declare a small type for the three values of a `place` line: `x0`, `baseline` and `scale`, as numbers that can be fractional or negative. It is a header with no `.cpp`.
jobs.src/render/Outline.h: Declare a drawing style (line thickness and marker size) and a function that draws one outline (the type from `GlyphComponent.h`) on your `FrameBufferCanvas`, given a placement, a style and a colour.
jobs.src/render/Outline.cpp: Implement it: turn every point into a pixel with the formulas in "From font units to pixels", join the points of each contour with lines, closing line included, then draw a marker on every point. Use your canvas's line and rectangle for both.

jobs.assignments/assignment_09_compound_glyph: On each `font` line, open the font and forget the earlier glyph locations; record each `glyph` line's offset and length by id. For each `decode` line, resolve the glyph and write the header line and one `ends` / `points` pair per part, as Output shows (fractional coordinates to at least 2 decimals).
jobs.src/font/CompoundGlyph.h: Declare a function that takes a glyph id, the font (through your `ByteReader`) and where every glyph's record is (offset and length, like the locations from your `Loca.h`), and returns a list of outlines in the form from `GlyphComponent.h`, one per simple part.
jobs.src/font/CompoundGlyph.cpp: Implement it with "The compound glyph record" and "Placing a component": an empty glyph gives no parts, and a simple glyph gives itself, decoded by your `GlyphParser` from assignment 07. For a compound glyph, read all of its component records, then resolve each component in record order, with its own transform applied first and the outer ones after.

jobs.assignments/assignment_10_bezier.cpp: Read the input file line by line: a `lerp` line gives two points and t, a `bezier` line gives the start, the control point, the end and t. Call your lerp or curve function from `utils/Geometry.h` and write one `x y` line per input line, with numbers as the Output section describes.
jobs.src/utils/Geometry.h: Declare a 2D point type with `double` x and y, and the arithmetic you want on it: adding, subtracting and scaling by a number. Write two functions on it: lerp, the point a fraction t of the way from a to b, and the point at t on a quadratic Bezier curve given its start, control point and end. There is no `Geometry.cpp`, so define the functions right here in the header and mark them `inline`.

jobs.assignments/assignment_11_outline_curves: Read the input as in assignment 08: make the canvas from the `canvas` line, keep the latest `place`, `style` (now only the line thickness) and `color`, and build each outline from its `ends` and `points` lines. Draw every outline with your new curve function from `render/Outline.h`, then write the canvas to the output path with your `FrameBufferCanvas` from assignment 06.
jobs.src/render/Outline.h: Add a second drawing function next to your straight-line one from assignment 08. It takes the canvas, an outline, its placement, a line thickness and a colour, and draws the outline with real curves. The Boilerplate's `Outline.h` already declares it as `renderGlyphCurves`; if you wrote the header your own way, add the declaration now.
jobs.src/render/Outline.cpp: Implement the curve drawing. Walk each contour from an on-curve point, turning the points into straight lines and quadratic curves (with an implied on-curve point between two off-curve points), and draw each curve as short lines using your curve function from `utils/Geometry.h`. Draw the red, green and blue markers only after all the lines of the outline.

jobs.assignments/assignment_12_segment_inters: Read each `segments` line as four points: a1 and a2 for segment A, then b1 and b2 for segment B. Call your intersection function from `utils/Geometry.h` and write the meeting point as `x y`, or `none`, one line per input line.
jobs.src/utils/Geometry.h: Add a function that takes two segments, each given by its two end points, and returns the one point where they meet, or nothing when they don't meet or are parallel or collinear (`std::optional` suits this). Small helpers for the 2D cross product and the side value belong here too, `inline` like the rest of the header. The Boilerplate's `Geometry.h` from assignment 10 already declares the function as `segmentsIntersect`.

13.title: Intersect a line and a quadratic curve

jobs.assignments/assignment_13_line_curve_int: Read each line as the curve's three points p1, p2 and p3 (start, control point, end), then the word `line` and the line's two points l1 and l2. Call your line-curve function from `utils/Geometry.h` and write the points it returns on one line (`x1 y1` or `x1 y1 x2 y2`), or `none` when there are none.
jobs.src/utils/Geometry.h: Add a function that takes a quadratic curve (start, control point, end) and two points on an infinite line, and returns the points where they meet: none, one or two, in increasing t. A dot product helper and a helper that solves a t^2 + b t + c = 0, the linear case a = 0 included, belong here too. The Boilerplate's `Geometry.h` from assignment 10 already declares the function as `segmentQuadBezierIntersect`.

Read the `canvas`, `place` and `color` lines and each `outline` with its `ends` and `points` lines (see Input). Make the canvas, fill every outline in turn with your even-odd fill, and write the picture to the output path (see Output).
jobs.src/render/Scanline.h: Declare what both fill rules share: a type for an edge piece (a straight line or a quadratic curve, in pixels) and one for a crossing (its x, and whether the edge runs up or down the screen there, which assignment 16 needs). Then declare functions that turn an outline and its placement into edge pieces, give each pixel row its crossings sorted by x, and fill a stretch of one row.
jobs.src/render/Scanline.cpp: Implement those three steps. Building the edges makes implied on-curve points explicit, starts each contour at an on-curve point and splits every curve where its y turns around. Scanning a row finds where the line through its pixel centres crosses each piece (by the half-open rule) and sorts the crossings, and filling a stretch paints the pixels whose centres lie in it, clipped to the canvas.
jobs.src/render/EvenOdd.h: Declare one function that fills an outline on a canvas by the even-odd rule, given its placement and colour.
jobs.src/render/EvenOdd.cpp: Implement it with your `render/Scanline`: build the edge pieces, then on every row fill from the 1st crossing to the 2nd, the 3rd to the 4th, and so on.

15.title: Lowest point of a quadratic curve

jobs.assignments/assignment_15_bezier_min_y.c: Read each `curve` line's six numbers as three points, call your lowest-point function, and write one answer per curve, in the same order (see Output for the precision).
jobs.src/utils/Geometry.h: Add a function that takes a quadratic curve's start, control and end points and returns the smallest y on the curve for t from 0 to 1, as an exact `double` (don't round it to a whole number). The Boilerplate from assignment 10 already declares it as `getBezierMinY`; if you wrote this file your own way, add it next to your curve functions.

Read the `canvas`, `place` and `color` lines and each `outline` with its `ends` and `points` lines (see Input). Make the canvas, fill every outline in turn with your non-zero fill, and write the picture to the output path (see Output).
jobs.src/render/NonZero.h: Declare one function that fills an outline on a canvas by the non-zero rule, given its placement and colour.
jobs.src/render/NonZero.cpp: Implement it with your `render/Scanline`: on every row, walk the sorted crossings left to right with a running winding count and fill each stretch where the count isn't zero. Each crossing needs the direction of its edge; if your crossings from assignment 14 don't record it yet, add it to `render/Scanline` first.

jobs.assignments/assignment_17_nonzero_curves: Read the `canvas`, `place` and `color` lines and each `outline` with its `ends` and `points` lines, where points can now be `off` (see Input). Make the canvas, fill every outline in turn with your non-zero fill, and write the picture to the output path (see Output).
jobs.src/render/NonZero.h: Keep the same fill function: from now on it also gets outlines with off-curve points, so curves. There is nothing new to declare unless you add a helper for curves.
jobs.src/render/NonZero.cpp: Make the non-zero fill right for curved outlines: every crossing on a curve needs the direction the curve runs at that row, which is easy once each curve is split where its y turns around. If your `render/Scanline` from assignment 14 already splits curves and gives every crossing its direction, your assignment 16 fill may pass as it is; otherwise add what's missing (in `render/Scanline` or here).

jobs.assignments/assignment_18_render_text.cp: Read the input line by line (see Input): load the font on `font`, make the canvas on `canvas`, keep the pen and colour from `pen` and `color`, and draw each `text` line (everything after `text` and its space) with your `TextRenderer`, carrying the returned pen x on to the next `text` line. Then write the picture to the output path (see Output).
jobs.src/utils/Unicode.h: Provide a function that decodes a string of UTF-8 bytes into a list of code points, for characters of 1 to 4 bytes (the byte patterns are under Output, step 1). It is small enough to live entirely in the header.
jobs.src/TextRenderer.h: Declare a class that loads a font from a path once and keeps what drawing needs: the map from code point to glyph, where each glyph's record is, and the advance widths. Give it a function that draws a UTF-8 string on a canvas from a pen x, baseline, scale and colour and returns the pen x after the last character, plus, for `main.cpp`, a way to measure a string's width and to read the font's ascent and descent.
jobs.src/TextRenderer.cpp: Implement the class by calling your earlier work: load the cmap (assignment 03), the glyph locations (04) and the advance widths (05) once, when the font is opened. To draw, decode the text, then for each code point find its glyph (glyph 0 if the font has none), fill each of its outlines from your `font/CompoundGlyph` with your non-zero fill, and move the pen by its advance times the scale.
jobs.src/main.cpp: Write the command-line program: take the font path, the text and the output path (and an optional pixel height) from the command line, size a canvas to fit the text, draw it in white with your `TextRenderer` and save the PNG. The checker doesn't run it, and the Boilerplate has it written; build the `tiny_ttf` target and try it on your own text.
